pages.title: Voltage drop from the intake, refined
pages.for: Enough voltage must reach the load. Keep the drop from the origin to the far end of the circuit within 3% for lighting or 5% for other circuits, on a public supply. BS 7671 takes the percentage of the nominal voltage. In your assessments, take it of the voltage given.
pages.rule:
VD = mV/A/m × Ib × L ÷ 1000
Total = submain + final circuit, from the intake
3-phase submain, 1-phase circuit: submain ÷ √3
Limit, public supply: lighting 3% (6.9 V 1-ph, 12 V 3-ph); others 5% (11.5 V, 20 V)
BS 7671: % of the nominal voltage. Assessments: % of the voltage given
Ct = (230 + tp − (Ca² Cg² − Ib²/It²)(tp − 30)) ÷ (230 + tp)
25 mm² and up, power factor known: r × cos φ + x × sin φ

Fails? Chase it with a bigger CSA, then try Ct on the size below it.
A three-phase load keeps every drop three-phase.
Check the Ct formula against Appendix 4 in your copy before you rely on it.

traps.text: Checking the final circuit on its own. The limit covers every drop from the intake to the end of the circuit.
traps.cite: Project guide p.6; formula sheet step 7

traps.cite: Slides p.40, 41; NAPIT, how to determine voltage drop limits, in research

traps.text: Dividing by √3 when the load is three-phase. The ÷ √3 is for a three-phase submain feeding a single-phase circuit.
Using z on 25 mm² and over when the power factor is known. It may overstate the drop.

traps.text: Leaving a cable chased up for voltage drop at its tabulated drop. It runs cooler, and with Ct a smaller cable may pass.

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text: Each drop is mV/A/m × Ib × L ÷ 1000. Keep the total from the origin to the far end within 3% for lighting or 5% for other circuits.
pages.alt: THE RULE VD = mV/A/m × Ib × L ÷ 1000 mV/A/m: the millivolts dropped for every ampere of design current for every metre of conductor. Ib: the design current, in amperes. L: the length, in metres. If it is skipped, or worked on one cable only: the load runs on less than it was designed for. A heater's power falls with the square of its voltage. A motor draws more current to keep its torque. A 3 kW heater on 85 m of 1.5 mm² drops 32.14 V, nearly three times the 11.50 V allowed.

The rule

VD = mV/A/m × Ib × L ÷ 1000

mV/A/m: the millivolts dropped for every ampere of design current for every metre of conductor. Ib: the design current, in amperes. L: the length, in metres.

pages.name: The why
pages.text: At 85 m the heater circuit drops 8.09 V. With the submain's 5.77 V the total is 13.86 V, over 11.50 V. The total reaches the limit near 60 m.

But with the submain's 5.77 V, the heater has lost 13.86 V from the origin. That is over 11.50 V, so its 216.14 V falls below 218.50 V. Heater circuit's drop 8.09 V Total from the origin 13.86 V Limit 11.50 V The submain's drop is line to line. The heater circuit runs line to neutral, a √3 smaller.

The submain's drop is line to line. The heater circuit runs line to neutral, a √3 smaller. So divide the submain's drop by √3 before adding: 10.00 ÷ √3 = 5.77 V. That leaves 224.23 V at the board. The drops add because the heater gets what is left of the origin's voltage after every cable it is fed through.

The Ct formula
Ct =230 + tp − (Ca² Cg² − Ib²/It²)(tp − 30)230 + tp

tp: the conductor's maximum operating temperature, 70 °C for PVC (thermoplastic), 90 °C for XLPE. Ca: the ambient temperature factor. Cg: the grouping factor. It: the tabulated current rating. Here tp is 70 °C, Ca 0.94 (0.94² = 0.8836) and Cg 1.

One way to picture Ib²/It²: heat goes with the square of the current. So 13.04 A in a cable rated 41 A makes about a tenth of its full-load heat.

Debated. Check this formula against Appendix 4 in your copy before you rely on it. Some read it as counting only the ambient temperature and grouping factors, so Ci is left out here. Ct earns its keep where Ib is well below It and few correction factors apply. In one example, with a grouping factor of 0.78 and nothing else, Ct was only about 0.99.

The showroom motor's is 0.8. φ z 1.65 Load's voltage Current r drop x drop z Shadows on the voltage At power factor 0.80, the r drop's shadow along the voltage is 1.28 and the x drop's is 0.16. In the picture, z is drawn from r and x: √(1.60² + 0.27²) = 1.62.

25 mm² 90 °C singles in conduit, three-phase: r 1.60, x 0.27 and z 1.65 mV/A/m (Table 4E1B). The showroom motor's is 0.8.

At power factor 1.00 the current is in step with the voltage. The whole r drop lies along it, and none of the x drop: 1.60 mV/A/m, just under z's 1.65.At power factor 0.80, the r drop's shadow along the voltage is 1.28 and the x drop's is 0.16. sin φ0.60
Drop per amp per metre1.44 mV/A/m
With a known power factor

Drop per amp per metre = r × cos φ + x × sin φ

cos φ is the power factor, and sin φ = √(1 − cos² φ).

In the picture, z is drawn from r and x: √(1.60² + 0.27²) = 1.62. The table's z, 1.65, is not exactly √(r² + x²). The tick marks the table's figure.

Why: the r drop is in step with the current, and the x drop is a quarter-cycle ahead. So only their parts along the load's voltage take away from its size. Taking z as if all of it lay along the voltage may give a drop higher than the actual one. r and x give an accurate figure for loads with a large inductive element. So a circuit may conform without being upsized. This lesson does not combine Ct with r and x.

pages.name: Section A (g)
pages.task: (g) Determine the actual voltage drop of the motor circuit, from the intake to the motor.
pages.alt: Your showroom: the motor SCENARIO A newly built car retailer; cars are driven over the showroom's concrete floor. Supply: three phase four wire 400 V, TN-C-S, Ze declared as 0.1 Ω, prospective fault current 4.6 kA; ambient 20 °C. Five boards: MDB, DBL1, DBL2, DBP1 and DBP2. In the consultation bay, a 400 V three-phase 11 kW motor, power factor 0.8 lagging, efficiency 86%, controlled by a star-delta starter and not subject to frequent starting and stopping. The cables from the starter to the motor are 90 °C thermosetting singles in conduit.
pages.html:
Your showroom: the motorScenario

A newly built car retailer; cars are driven over the showroom's concrete floor. Supply: three phase four wire 400 V, TN-C-S, Ze declared as 0.1 Ω, prospective fault current 4.6 kA; ambient 20 °C. Five boards: MDB, DBL1, DBL2, DBP1 and DBP2. In the consultation bay, a 400 V three-phase 11 kW motor, power factor 0.8 lagging, efficiency 86%, controlled by a star-delta starter and not subject to frequent starting and stopping. The cables from the starter to the motor are 90 °C thermosetting singles in conduit.

Your assignment ED4-01A: pack p.3, and question 4 on p.4.

Carried forward
(a)Motor's design current, Ib23.08 A
(b)Each winding, in delta13.33 A
(c)Breaker rating at DBP2 for the motor circuit25 A
(d)Minimum It of the starter-to-motor singles16.66 A
(e)The table and column for the starter-to-motor singlesTable 4E1A, column 5
(f)Minimum CSA of the starter-to-motor cables1.5 mm²

Assumed here: the motor is fed from DBP2, about 11.4 m along the walls on plan. That is approximate: a real design adds the vertical runs. DBP2 to the starter: 2.5 mm² 90 °C thermosetting singles in conduit, one three-phase circuit, 16 mV/A/m (Table 4E1B, column 6). Starter to motor: part (f)'s six 1.5 mm² singles, 3.0 m, a practice value. Measure the real run. They are 31 mV/A/m for two cables single-phase (column 3). The DBP2 submain's three-phase drop: 4.00 V, a practice value.

The leg: in delta running, the windings are three single-phase loads. Each is fed through two of the six conductors, one at each end. Each conductor carries the winding current, 13.33 A (part b). We take the leg's drop as 31 × 13.33 × 3.0 ÷ 1000, line to line, and add it to the rest. That reading is ours, not BS 7671's, and it is debated. Some multiply by √3 as well, which gives 2.15 V here.

16 × 23.08 × 11.4 ÷ 1000 = 4.21 V; 31 × 13.33 × 3.0 ÷ 1000 = 1.24 V; 4.00 + 4.21 + 1.24 = 9.45 V ≤ 20.00 V (2.36%). These are practice values. There is no ÷ √3, because the motor is three-phase.

Refined with Ct

The 2.5 mm² cable carries 23.08 A of its 28 A (Table 4E1A, column 5). Take tp as 90 °C, Ca as 1.00, a practice value, and Cg as 1. Then Ct is 0.94, giving 3.96 V. The leg has Cg 0.80 and It 20 A. Its Ct is 0.96, giving 1.19 V. In all that is 9.15 V. It is not needed, since 9.45 V passes.

DBP2 cable: (23.08 ÷ 28)² = 0.6794; 1 − 0.6794 = 0.3206; × 60 = 19.24; (320 − 19.24) ÷ 320 = 0.9399, Ct 0.94; 4.21 × 0.94 = 3.96 V. Leg: 0.64 − (13.33 ÷ 20)² = 0.64 − 0.4442 = 0.1958; × 60 = 11.75; (320 − 11.75) ÷ 320 = 0.9633, Ct 0.96; 1.24 × 0.96 = 1.19 V. 4.00 + 3.96 + 1.19 = 9.15 V

The power factor comes in only from 25 mm² up, so it is left out here.

Set out like a City & Guilds 2396 Section A question, on the showroom motor.

pages.name: Section B
pages.task: Explain why a cable carrying well under its rating drops less voltage than Appendix 4's mV/A/m gives, and how a designer can take credit for it.
pages.why: A model answer: Appendix 4's mV/A/m values assume the conductor is at its maximum operating temperature, 70 °C or 90 °C. It reaches that only when it carries its full load. Current heats a conductor, and a hotter conductor has more resistance, so more drop. A cable carrying well under its rating, Ib well below It, runs cooler. So its resistance and its drop are lower than the table says. The designer takes credit with the factor Ct, which multiplies the tabulated drop. Ct is worked from Ib and It, the maximum operating temperature, and the ambient and grouping factors. It can let a smaller cable pass. A 3 kW heater in 4.0 mm² drops 12.19 V by the table but 10.97 V with Ct, inside the 11.50 V limit.

pages.name: Changed numbers
pages.task: A single-phase power circuit, 32 m of 1.5 mm² 90 °C singles in conduit (31 mV/A/m), Ib 9 A, is fed from a sub-board whose three-phase submain drops 7.5 V. No supply voltage is given. Determine the total voltage drop from the origin.
pages.alt: The same kind of question, with new numbers. 31 × 9 × 32 ÷ 1000 = 8.93 V; 7.5 ÷ √3 = 4.33 V; 4.33 + 8.93 = 13.26 V > 11.50 V. It fails, though the circuit alone would pass.
